population: single healthy male volunteer (self-experiment by the study's own physician)

vd_assumed_or_fitted: fitted/measured: Vd = absorbed dose / back-extrapolated C0
exposure_ceased: yes by design - a single bolus dose, so intake is exactly known and zero thereafter; the 13C label also removes background interference entirely
background_adjusted: not needed for the labelled compounds (13C-label separates them from background); for MPFOA a pre-existing level of 0.130 ug/L was subtracted; PFBS, 6:2FTS, HFPO-DA and DONA were unlabelled

model: two-compartment (one-compartment for MPFBA and 6:2FTS); terminal phase t1/2 = ln2/kel; CLtot = kel x Vd
estimation_basis_serumdecay_or_massbalan: both - plasma decay for the half-life and Vd, plus a full urinary and faecal mass balance for clearance

CRITICAL: only 107.66 half-lives were actually observed in the 450-day window, so the long-chain values are extrapolations from the early terminal slope, not observed decay. Clearance partition: CLuri 1.00, CLtot 1.24 mL/min; fup 0.093; CLfilt 10.57; faecal not detected.
risk_of_bias_notes: n=1, male, 67 y - no inter-individual variability, no sex contrast, no generalisability. BUT this is the ONLY human study with a known administered dose, a label that eliminates background, and simultaneous urinary and faecal measurement, so it is the only design that needs no assumption about exposure cessation or background. For the project's core question: plasma C0 here was 0.13-1.64 ug/L, i.e. 30-500x BELOW the serum levels of every contaminated-community cohort, and the PFOA half-life came out at 5.5 y against 2.3-3.2 y in those cohorts - the direction saturable reabsorption predicts, though confounded by the extrapolation and by n=1.

key_assumptions: 'In all the included studies, PFAS half-life was estimated using one-compartment models with first-order elimination.' So every study in the systematic review shares the same structural assumption, and the heterogeneity (I2 up to 97%) arises entirely from design and population, not from model choice. As of Oct 2026 the only human PFAS half-life estimates NOT from a one-compartment first-order model are Chiu 2022 (Bayesian hierarchical one-compartment, still first-order) and Abraham 2024 (two-compartment). No human PBPK model has been used to estimate a half-life from primary data; Worley 2017's PBPK analysis was used to reconstruct exposure, and the F-53B PBPK model (Zhang 2024, PMID 39394996) extrapolates from pregnant mice.
risk_of_bias_notes: A systematic structural assumption shared by 13 of 13 studies cannot be detected by any between-study comparison, including this meta-analysis.

key_assumptions: Half-lives: 25.8 d at 397 ng/mL, 43.8 d at 0.33 ng/mL, 50.6 d at 1.64 ng/mL. Treating clearance as proportional to 1/t1/2 at constant Vd, the log-log slope over a 1,200-fold concentration range is about +0.12. This is the cleanest cross-study concentration test available for any PFAS, because PFBS has no background to subtract, all three studies had verified cessation, all three used first-order models, and all three observed 1-7 half-lives rather than a fraction of one. Xu 2020's own text raises the same inference: 'Given the large variation in exposure levels between the two studies, a dose-dependency of PFBS serum elimination half-life cannot be ruled out.'
risk_of_bias_notes: Three points, three different laboratories, n<=17 each, and the 0.33 vs 1.64 ng/mL pair runs the WRONG way (lower concentration, shorter half-life), so the slope is carried entirely by the Olsen point. Not an estimate - a sanity check. It is, however, remarkably close to the +0.11 log-log slope the project measured in male rats for PFOA and to the +0.09 cross-human-cohort slope in literature/human_dose_test.py.

risk_of_bias_notes: CENTRAL METHODOLOGICAL FINDING FOR THE EXPOSURE-LEVEL QUESTION. Because this bias is large at low exposure and negligible at high exposure, any regression of apparent half-life on exposure level that pools background-corrected and uncorrected studies will produce a SPURIOUS NEGATIVE slope - low-exposure cohorts will appear to eliminate more slowly. That is exactly the signature a saturable-reabsorption mechanism would also produce, so the two are confounded in every cross-cohort comparison. They can only be separated within a study that reports both corrections, and in those studies (Li 2022 Table S4, Batzella 2024 quartiles, Lyu 2026 Table 4, Xu 2020 Spearman tests) the residual concentration effect is either absent or runs the opposite way.
